title: Weather, Soil and Farm Problems
hint: Drought, flood, frost, pests; because of, due to, lead to; if it doesn't rain, if we had more water
why: weather and farming are in the news all the time: dry summers, floods, storms and food prices. To understand these stories and talk about them, you need the words for weather problems and clear ways to say what causes what, and what will or would happen.
know: weather problems: drought, flood, frost, hail, heatwave, storm
soil and crop words: fertile, erosion, irrigation, pest, weed, disease, yield, a good or poor harvest
cause and effect phrases: because of, due to, so, as a result, lead to, cause
understand: why we say because of the drought but because it didn't rain
the difference between If it doesn't rain, the crops will die (real and possible) and If we had more water, we would grow more (not true now, imagined)
able: describe a weather problem and its effects on farms and food
explain causes and results in simple, clear sentences
talk about what will happen, and what you would do, in different situations
mistakes: Because of it didn't rain, the crops died.
Because it didn't rain, the crops died. / Because of the drought, ...
If it will rain tomorrow, the farmers will be happy.
If it rains tomorrow, the farmers will be happy.
If we would have more water, we would grow more.
If we had more water, we would grow more.
The drought caused that the crops died.
The drought caused the crops to die. / The drought killed the crops.
The storm lead to flooding last week.
The storm led to flooding last week.
The soil here is very fertility.
warmup: What was the weather like where you live this year? Was there any extreme weather?
What kind of weather is bad for farmers? Why?
Have food prices in your country changed because of the weather? Which foods?

rows: drought
a long time with little or no rain
The drought lasted three months.
flood / flooding
a lot of water covering land that is usually dry
The fields were under water after the flood.
frost
a thin white layer of ice on the ground on a cold night
A late frost damaged the apple blossom.
hail
small balls of ice that fall like rain
The hail broke the greenhouse windows.
heatwave
a period of very hot weather
During the heatwave it was 38°C.
storm
very strong wind, often with heavy rain
The storm blew the roof off the barn.
soil
the top layer of earth where plants grow
Potatoes like light, sandy soil.
fertile (noun: fertility)
good for growing plants
The valley has very fertile soil.
erosion
when wind or water slowly carries soil away
Trees and hedges help to stop erosion.
irrigation (verb: irrigate)
bringing water to fields with pipes or channels
Without irrigation, nothing grows here in summer.
pest
an insect or animal that damages crops
Slugs are a common garden pest.
weed
a wild plant growing where you don't want it
We pull up the weeds every week.
disease
an illness of plants or animals
A disease killed half the potato plants.
yield
how much a field or crop produces
The wheat yield was high this year.
a good / poor harvest; crop failure
a lot / not much food was collected; the crop didn't grow
After the drought there was a poor harvest.
because of / due to + noun
the cause (a thing)
The harvest was late because of the rain. The road is closed due to flooding.
because + subject + verb
the cause (a sentence)
The harvest was late because it rained a lot.
so / As a result,
the result
It was very dry, so the grass turned brown. As a result, hay prices went up.
cause + noun / lead to + noun
a cause and its result in one sentence
Frost can cause damage. Heavy rain can lead to floods.
If + present, ... will + verb
a real, possible future (first conditional)
If it doesn't rain soon, the crops will fail.
If + past, ... would + verb
an imagined or unlikely situation (second conditional)
If we had more water, we would grow more.

say: drought rhymes with out (the gh is silent); flood rhymes with mud, not food; soil rhymes with oil; yield sounds like yeeld; eROsion, irriGAtion.

exercises.title: What's the problem?
exercises.intro: Match each word to its meaning. Tap a word, then tap its meaning.

items.r: a long time with little or no rain
items.why: A drought is a long period without enough rain. Plants and animals suffer.

items.r: water covering land that is usually dry
items.why: A flood happens when rivers or heavy rain put water on land that is normally dry.

items.r: thin ice on the ground after a cold night
items.why: Frost is a white layer of ice. A late frost in spring can kill young plants and fruit blossom.

items.r: small balls of ice that fall like rain
items.why: Hail is small balls of ice falling from the sky. It can damage crops, cars and windows.

items.r: a period of very hot weather
items.why: A heatwave is several days of very hot weather.

items.r: an insect or animal that damages crops
items.why: A pest is an insect or animal that eats or damages crops, like slugs or aphids.

items.r: a wild plant growing where you don't want it
items.why: A weed is a wild plant growing among the crops or in the garden.

items.r: bringing water to fields with pipes
items.why: Irrigation means bringing water to fields with pipes, sprinklers or channels.
Before a noun (the drought), use because of. Because needs a subject and verb.

items.pre: It didn't rain for three months,
items.why: So introduces the result: no rain, so the grass turned brown.

items.pre: The roads near the farm were closed
items.why: Due to + noun gives the cause, like because of: due to flooding.

items.pre: The heavy rain washed away the soil.
items.post: , the field is now full of stones.
items.why: As a result starts a new sentence about the result, followed by a comma.
Cause + noun: frost can cause damage. Lead needs to: lead to damage.
The phrase is lead to + noun: lead to plant diseases.
First conditional: if + present simple, then will. If it doesn't rain soon, the crops will die.

items.why: Second conditional: if + past, then would + verb. If they had more water, they would grow more.

items.why: The yield is how much a field or crop produces.

exercises.title: Reading
exercises.text:
Dry summer hits local farmers

Farmers in the Fraser Valley say this has been the driest summer for thirty years. Only 12 millimetres of rain fell in July and August, compared with 90 millimetres in a normal year.

“The soil is like dust,” says dairy farmer Ken Dhaliwal. “The grass stopped growing in July, so we're already feeding the cows the hay we saved for winter.” As a result, many farmers will have to buy extra hay, and prices have doubled.

Vegetable growers have done better because most of them use irrigation. But water is now a problem too. Due to low river levels, the town has asked farms to water their fields only at night.

Fruit farmer Maria Santos lost part of her blueberry crop in a heatwave in early August. “If it doesn't rain soon, the plants will suffer next year too,” she says. “If we had a bigger pond, we would store more water in the winter. That's our plan now.”

Forecasters expect rain next week.
exercises.intro: Read the news article. Then type the missing word from the text, and press Check.

items.ask: How much rain fell in July and August?
items.why: Paragraph 1: 'Only 12 millimetres of rain fell in July and August.'

items.ask: What are Ken's cows eating now?
items.why: Paragraph 2: 'we're already feeding the cows the hay we saved for winter.'

items.ask: Why have vegetable growers done better?
items.why: Paragraph 3: 'Vegetable growers have done better because most of them use irrigation.'

items.ask: When can farms water their fields now?
items.why: Paragraph 3: the town has asked farms 'to water their fields only at night'.

items.ask: What would help Maria store more water?
items.why: Paragraph 4: 'If we had a bigger pond, we would store more water in the winter.'

exercises.title: Speaking
items: What is the worst weather you remember? What happened, and what were the results?
Which weather problems are common in your country: drought, floods, frost, storms? How do they affect farmers and food prices?
If there was no rain for three months where you live, what would happen? What would you do differently?
If you had a small farm or garden, what would you grow? What problems do you think you would have?

parts.rule:
Watch out

  • + a noun: because of the rain, due to the drought, as a result of the storm, led to floods, caused damage
  • + a sentence (subject and verb): because it rained, so the grass died, if it rains, As a result, prices went up
parts.intro: What comes after each phrase? Sort them.

chips.why: Because of + noun: because of the drought.
Due to + noun: due to heavy rain.
As a result of + noun: as a result of the storm.
Lead to + noun: The rain led to floods.
Cause + noun: The frost caused damage.
Because + subject + verb: because it didn't rain.
So + subject + verb: so the grass died.
If + subject + verb: if it rains tomorrow.
As a result, + subject + verb: As a result, prices went up.
Since (= because) + subject + verb: since it was so dry.

items.q: If it will be sunny tomorrow, we'll cut the hay.
items.why: First conditional: no will after if. If it is sunny tomorrow, we'll cut the hay.

items.q: The crops died because of it was too hot.
items.why: Before a subject and verb (it was), use because, not because of.

items.q: If I had more land, I would grow apples.
items.why: Correct: second conditional, if + past, would + verb.
Lead needs to before the result: Heavy rain can lead to flooding.

items.q: The soil here is very fertility.
items.why: After very, use the adjective fertile. Fertility is the noun.

teacher.purpose: give general learners the language of weather problems and their effects on farms and food (drought, flood, frost, hail, heatwave, pest, erosion, yield, a poor harvest), clear cause-and-effect phrases (because of, due to, so, as a result, lead to, cause), and the first and second conditionals for real and imagined situations. It prepares students to follow and discuss news stories about weather and food.
teacher.before: find a short, recent news headline or photo about extreme weather and farming in the student's country or yours (a drought, a flood, a frost on fruit trees). It makes the warm-up and speaking real.
plan: The three warm-up questions, or show your headline first. Note how the student links ideas: do they use because and so, or only and?

Weather problems first (draw quick pictures: sun and cracked ground, rain and water, ice). Then soil and crops. Then the cause and effect table: make one chain together: No rain → dry soil → poor harvest → higher prices.
Matching, then the connectors and conditionals. In Exercise 2, ask “Is a noun or a sentence after the gap?”
Do one together and set the other for home.

The news article. First ask: “Who had the biggest problem: the dairy farmer, the vegetable growers or the fruit farmer?” Then the questions. Ask the student to find one so, one as a result, one due to and both conditionals.
Questions 2 and 3 are the core. Push for chains of causes: “And what happened because of that?”
Cause and effect and wrap-up (4 min).
Exercise 7 Part A together; Part B at home.
pron: drought /draʊt/: rhymes with out. Students often say /drɒt/ or /drɔːt/ because of bought, thought.
soil /sɔɪl/: one syllable with the oi of boy. hail /heɪl/ sounds the same as hale.
fertile: UK /ˈfɜːtaɪl/, North America /ˈfɜːrtl/. Both are correct.
erosion /ɪˈrəʊʒn/ and irrigation /ˌɪrɪˈɡeɪʃn/: the -sion in erosion is the sound in television.
mistakes: because vs because of: the most common error in this lesson. Quick test: if there is a verb after it, use because.
due to works like because of: due to the rain. Not due to it rained.
cause: cause + noun (caused damage) or cause + someone/something + to + verb (caused the river to rise). Not caused that (a direct translation from Spanish causó que, French a fait que).
lead / led: the past is led, pronounced like the metal lead /led/. Students often write lead for the past.
No will after if in the first conditional: If it rains, not If it will rain. In the second conditional, no would after if: If we had, not If we would have.
weather is uncountable: bad weather, not a bad weather. hail and flooding are uncountable; a flood and a storm are countable.
plague vs pest: Spanish plaga, French parasite / nuisible. In English a plague is a big disaster (a plague of locusts); a normal insect problem is a pest.
uk_us: Same word, different spelling. The site uses -ise; both are fine.
A rule that stops people watering gardens in a drought.
1 hectare is about 2.5 acres. Canadian farmers often still talk in acres.
adapt: Focus on drought, flood, frost, storm, heatwave, soil, pest, weed, harvest; because, because of, so; first conditional.
Add erosion, yield, crop failure, fertility, as a result of, consequently, resulting in, and the second conditional for policy ideas (If the government paid farmers to plant trees, ...).
Describe one weather event and its effects with because and so.
Discuss a news story: causes, effects on prices and people, and what you would do if you were a farmer or a minister.
teacher.extra:
A quick check: real or imagined?

If the student mixes the two conditionals, ask “Is it possible, or are you imagining?”

  • If it rains tomorrow, ...: possible; it might really happen → will.
  • If I had a farm, ...: imagined; I don't have one → would.
prompts: The worst weather you remember. Follow up: “What happened because of it?” “What was the result for people near you?” Listen for because of + sentence.
Weather problems in your country. Follow up: “What happens to food prices after a drought?” “Which crops suffer most?” Good for lead to and as a result.
No rain for three months. Second conditional practice. Follow up: “What would happen to the parks? To water bills? Would you change your habits?”
Your own farm or garden. Follow up: “What pests would you have?” “What would you do if a frost came in May?” Mix first and second conditionals.

bank.q: The village was cut off for two days ___ the floods.
bank.why: Due to + noun gives the cause: due to the floods.

bank.q: There was a frost last night, ___ the young plants are black this morning.
bank.why: So introduces the result: a frost, so the plants are black.

bank.q: If the weather ___ dry next week, they will start the harvest.
bank.why: First conditional: if + present simple. If the weather stays dry, they will start.

bank.q: If I ___ a garden, I would grow my own tomatoes.
bank.why: Second conditional for an imagined situation: if + past, would + verb.

bank.q: Too much water in the soil can ___ the roots to rot.
bank.why: Cause + something + to + verb: cause the roots to rot.

bank.q: A long period with no rain is called a ___.
bank.why: A drought is a long time with little or no rain.

bank.q: Farmers use sprays to protect their crops from ___ such as insects and slugs.
bank.why: Pests are insects or animals that damage crops.

bank.q: The wheat ___ was lower than last year because of the wet spring.
bank.why: The yield is how much a crop produces.

bank.q: A sudden ___ storm covered the cars with small balls of ice.
bank.why: Hail is small balls of ice that fall like rain: a hail storm.

bank.q: In a ___, the temperature stays above 30 degrees for several days.
bank.why: A heatwave is a period of very hot weather.

bank.q: Wild plants that grow between the vegetables are called ___.
bank.why: Weeds are wild plants growing where you don't want them.

bank.q: If we don't water the plants, they ___ die.
bank.why: First conditional: if + present, then will + verb.

bank.q: The heavy rain led ___ landslides in the hills.
bank.why: Lead to + noun: The heavy rain led to landslides.

bank.q: If it will snow tonight, the roads will be dangerous.
bank.why: No will after if in the first conditional: If it snows tonight, ...

bank.q: The farmers lost half their crop because of the hail.
bank.why: Correct: because of + noun (the hail).

bank.q: If I would live in the country, I would keep chickens.
bank.why: Second conditional: if + past simple. If I lived in the country, I would keep chickens.

bank.q: The dry weather lead to a poor harvest last year.
bank.why: Last year needs the past: lead, led, led. The dry weather led to a poor harvest.

bank.a: The river flooded because of the heavy rain.
bank.why: Result + because of + noun: The river flooded because of the heavy rain.

bank.a: If it gets colder, the pond will freeze.
alt: The pond will freeze if it gets colder.
bank.why: First conditional: If + present, will + verb.

bank.a: What would you do if your crops failed?
bank.why: Second conditional question: What would you do + if + past?
